messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Support for circular distributions
messages.body_plain:
On 10/30/12 6:52 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, October 30, 2012 3:41:00 PM UTC-4, Daniel Mitchell wrote:

>     I also wonder if, given von_mises_log(y, mu, kappa), I should use something like fmod to silently translate y and mu
>     to the support interval, or if it would be better to issue an error.
>
> Here, I think that an exception should be thrown outside the support and have the message mention the correct bounds. If
> we permit unrestricted input and do some mod thing internally, then the posterior is technically improper, right?

For now, you should implement it like the other distributions.

We may make wholesale changes to them at some point, because
we're in the middle of rethinking the following behaviors:

   - prob functions (pdf, pmf) with variates out of bound
   - prob functions with parameters out of bounds
   - cumulative distribution functions with params out of bounds
   - cumulative distributions with variates out of support

   - same again at limits of support or parameter definendess (e.g., scale = 0)

and whether to just:

   - return NaN
   - return -infinity
   - raise an exception

None of this really matters for Stan models as they all have the
same effect of causing the current position to be Metropolis
rejected by the sampler.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: [stan-users] Re: employing a ragged array of cutpoints
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: [stan-users] Re: employing a ragged array of cutpoints
messages.body_plain:
On 10/29/12 4:09 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> (Moving to stan-dev.)
>
> I think this also relates to the older question of being able to
> inspect the length of an array and not having to specify it as a
> separate variable. It'd be really nice to be able to write something
> like
> data {
>    int[int[]] x;
> }
> model {
>    for (i in 1:x.size)
>      for (j in 1:x[i].size)
>        x ~ normal(mu, 1);
> }
> to load an Rdump that looks like
> x <-
> list(c(1, 2, 3), 1, c(2, 8))

It's much easier to see how to do this in the data { ... } block
than elsewhere.  The data gets read out of a structured file
that declares dimensions (albeit inconveniently postifx).

The model transforms a vector of parameters into structured
parameters.  I don't know how to do that without declared
sizes for structures.

For data, we'd need to rewrite the io/reader.hpp code to
just buffer all the input until it got to the dimension
declarations, then construct an object based on dims
or total number of objects read into which to write.

You can already do the following in Stan:

    for (i in 1:size(x))
      for (j in 1:size(x[i]))
         ...

I'd rather see a declaration that matched our
regular syntax like:

   int x[,];

Now we COULD start generalizing all of our syntax so
it doesn't mix the syntax into the variable names like C
does.  So for Stan 2.0, we could support a new format of:

   int[5,3] x;

instead of the current:

   int x[5,3];

or we could support both formats and even a mix of both
with

   int[3] x[5]

or even

    vector[2][3,4] x[5,6,7];

- Bob

make clean-all && make -j8 CC=clang++ /tmp/SU/parser/normal 2>/tmp/parser.log
grep "line=9" /tmp/parser.log

and a successful return code of grep would define the git bisect good state.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: [stan-users] Re: employing a ragged array of cutpoints
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: [stan-users] Re: employing a ragged array of cutpoints
messages.body_plain:
I think just having it in the data block would be fine. I can imagine
a couple of approaches to dealing with ragged parameter arrays. One
looks something like this:

data {
  int x[,];
}
parameters {
  float z[size(x),];

  for (i in 1:size(x))

    z[i].resize(size(x[i]));
}

and another looks something like this:

data {
  int x[,];
}
parameters {
  float z[x];
}

The second is pithier, but maybe more confusing. The first puts the
responsibility of defining array shapes on the user. Because the code
is in the parameters block, we only have to run it once, just after
we've read in the data and know what the shapes should be.

Matt

On Thu, Nov 1, 2012 at 12:24 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>
> On 10/29/12 4:09 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>>
>> (Moving to stan-dev.)
>>
>> I think this also relates to the older question of being able to
>> inspect the length of an array and not having to specify it as a
>> separate variable. It'd be really nice to be able to write something
>> like
>> data {
>>    int[int[]] x;
>> }
>> model {
>>    for (i in 1:x.size)
>>      for (j in 1:x[i].size)
>>        x ~ normal(mu, 1);
>> }
>> to load an Rdump that looks like
>> x <-
>> list(c(1, 2, 3), 1, c(2, 8))
>
>
> It's much easier to see how to do this in the data { ... } block
> than elsewhere.  The data gets read out of a structured file
> that declares dimensions (albeit inconveniently postifx).
>
> The model transforms a vector of parameters into structured
> parameters.  I don't know how to do that without declared
> sizes for structures.
>
> For data, we'd need to rewrite the io/reader.hpp code to
> just buffer all the input until it got to the dimension
> declarations, then construct an object based on dims
> or total number of objects read into which to write.
>
> You can already do the following in Stan:
>
>    for (i in 1:size(x))
>      for (j in 1:size(x[i]))
>         ...
>
>
> I'd rather see a declaration that matched our
> regular syntax like:
>
>   int x[,];
>
> Now we COULD start generalizing all of our syntax so
> it doesn't mix the syntax into the variable names like C
> does.  So for Stan 2.0, we could support a new format of:
>
>   int[5,3] x;
>
> instead of the current:
>
>   int x[5,3];
>
> or we could support both formats and even a mix of both
> with
>
>   int[3] x[5]
>
> or even
>
>    vector[2][3,4] x[5,6,7];
>
> - Bob
>

> --
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Ben, could you run the meta traits tests?

Bob and I committed 07f07f6012d5 <https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/detail?r=07f07f6012d5b19e9d1a12f82d61f711e4b85829>. There are a couple ways we think the tests could fail. If one of the tests fail, I think that's enough information to figure out what's happening on a linux box.

Daniel

On Sat, Oct 27, 2012 at 6:12 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> 1.  This is only going to affect behavior that's
> not yet documented in the manual -- vectorizing matrices,
> for instance,  m ~ normal(0,1) to give a whole matrix
> m a unit normal distirbution.
>
> 2.  The failing part of the test is here:
>
> and here's the test from:
>
> test/meta/traits_test.cpp, line 227:
> -------------------------
>   const Matrix<double,1,Dynamic> d(c);
>   VectorView<const Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> > dv(d);
>   for (size_t n = 0; n < 10; ++n)
>     EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(d[n], dv[n]);
> --------------------------
>
> I'm pretty sure the problem is the way the VectorView
> templates are getting instantiated.   Here is the
> basic class:
>
>
>   template<typename T,
>            bool is_vec = stan::is_vector<T>::value>
>   class VectorView
>
> and here are its specializations:
>
>   template<typename T>
>   class VectorView<T*,false>
>
>   template<typename T>
>   class VectorView<T,true>
>
>   template<typename T>
>   class VectorView<T*,true>
>
>   template<typename T>
>   class VectorView<const T,true>
>
> The only one that matches the call in the test should
> be the last one, but the behavior looks like the basic
> class might be getting instantiated.
>
> Also, I think trying to instantiate VectorView<double*>
> would lead to a conflict betwene the first and third
> template specialization.
>
>
> Also, the basic class's definition seems wrong, because
> it doesn't actually pay attention to the is_vec
> declaration and treats everything as a scalar ptr.
>
> stan/meta/traits.hpp, line 171
> -------------------------------
>   template<typename T,
>            bool is_vec = stan::is_vector<T>::value>
>   class VectorView {
>   private:
>     T* x_;
>   public:
>     VectorView(T& x) : x_(&x) { }
>     typename scalar_type<T>::type& operator[](int /*i*/) {
>       return *x_;
>     }
>   };
> ---------------
>
> The is_vec gets a default, but isn't used in the class definition.
> Instead, the operator[] definition assumes T is not a vector.
>
> I think the problem might go away if we change the basic class so
> that its operator[] definition is:
>
>     typename scalar_type<T>::type& operator[](int i) {
>       if (is_vec) return x_[i];
>       else return *x_;
>     }
>
> AND
>
> add Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic> to the is_vector type.  Or
> maybe better, an is_vector<T> || is_matrix<T> so we can
> keep the types separate.
>
> The (is_vec) value is known statically, so should get optimized away
> in the two instances of the template (is_vec = TRUE, is_vec = FALSE).
>
> Alternatively, I think it could be rewritten.  As is, there
> are probably unexpected consequences of the definitions such
> as the fact that const types are always assumed to be vectors.
>
> Is the behavior we want just this?
>
>   scalar-like:   double,              var
>
>   vector-like:   double*,             var*,
>                  vector<double>,      vector<var>,
>                  Matrix<double,R,C>,  Matrix<var,R,C>
>
> Reference types T& should behave like the unreferenced type T.
> Usually in this kind of setup, so do pointers, but here the
> decision was made to treat pointers as arrays.
>
> But we should be able to fix this problem by simply defining
> vector views for all these types:
>
> basic, def for scalars:
>
>    template <typename T> VectorView
>
> vector-like def:
>
>    template <typename T> VectorView<T*>
>
>    template <typename T> VectorView<vector<T> >
>
>    template <typename T, int R, int C> VectorView<Matrix<T,R,C> >
>
> Of course, we really only need two definitions for vector view,
> one for scalars and one for vectors.  We could instead have a bunch
> of factory functions that return VectorView instances rather than
> definining a bunch of VectorView template classes with redundant
> definitions.
>
> Daniel -- if this is all too much to digest, we can talk on Monday.

>
>
> - Bob
>
> --
>
>

It seems that stanc error message is still not as good as in 1.0.2.  For
example, in 1.0.3,

$ more a.stan
model {
   y ~ normal();
}

$ ./bin/stanc a.stan
Model name=a_model
Input file=a.stan
Output file=a_model.cpp

INVALID COMMAND-LINE ARGUMENT
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=a.stan; line=2, column=3

   y ~ normal();
   ^-- here

Execute "stanc --help" for more information
$ ./bin/stanc --version
stanc version 1.0.3

And I guess it should not say `INVALID COMMAND-LINE ARGUMENT` and
`Execute "stanc --help" for more information.`
For the same wrong coded a.stan, 1.0.2 reports

$ more a.stan
model {
   y ~ normal();
}

$ ./bin/stanc --version
stanc version 1.0.2
$ ./bin/stanc a.stan
Model name=a_model
Input file=a.stan
Output file=a_model.cpp

ERROR PARSING
LOCATION:  file=a.stan; line=2, column=3

   y ~ normal();
   ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

variable "y" does not exist.
Parser expecting: "}"

OUTPUT FILE REMOVED, file=a_model.cpp

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] cppcheck
messages.body_plain:
Bottom line is that there was nothing significant wrong
with our code but a few places where the style was improved
(in my opinion -- they don't call it "style" for nothing).

Most of the "error" reports have many instances, so I'll just
address one of each type.

0.  Too many ifdefs.
The tests just crap out and report after 12.

1.  Boost macros.
These look like errors on cppcheck's part in processing macros.

2.  Shifting by negative.
The number one false positive is this one from Eigen:

  y << -0.1, 0.0, 1.0;<--- Shifting by a negative value.

They clearly don't recognize that "<<" has been overridden
for y an Eigen::Matrix :-)

3.  Exception should be caught by reference.

These are in generated code for models, so it's good Ben checked
those, too.  An example is

   } catch (std::domain_error e) {
      throw std::domain_error(std::string("Invalid value of sigma: ") +
      std::string(e.what())); };<--- Exception should be caught by reference.

Our code should actually be OK here, but I changed
the generator to produce a reference anyway.

The reason to catch by reference is to avoid slicing
if you catch an instance of a subclass.  The code we
have should actually be OK because we don't have subclasses
of domain_error, but I changed it to a reference in
generator.hpp anyway.

4.  Unused variable.

These are in models.  It's just stylistic.   I could be
more clever in generating code, but it's really a pain to recurse
through the syntax to do the checks we'd need.

5.  Variable hiding.

It caught an issue with Google test, which presumably defines
some local variable "warmup" in an unobfuscated way.  I fixed this
by changing the name of the enum in our test to warmup_opt.

6.  Variable scope can be reduced.

Another very minor stylistic issue, but I fixed it to comply
anyway.

7.  log(0) called.

As far as I can tell, the C++ spec has this to say about the
argument to std::log():

   If it is zero, the function returns a negative HUGE_VAL and sets the value of the global variable
   errno to the ERANGE value.

So it's not a false positive per se.  It's in a test where
we're testing exactly this boundary behavior.

- Bob

messages.subject: Intel compiler
messages.body_plain:
Intel released the 2013 edition of its C++ compiler. You can get it from

http://software.intel.com/en-us/non-commercial-software-development

Stan seems to (still) work with it, although it is even worse than g++ in terms of compilation speed and RAM consumption.

You can make a rstan package by doing make install in the rstan/ director with something like this in ~/.R/Makevars

CC=icc
CXX=icpc

CXXFLAGS = -O3 -pipe -mp $(LTO)  #set_by_rstan
R_XTRA_CPPFLAGS =  -I$(R_INCLUDE_DIR) -DNDEBUG  #set_by_rstan

ICC_LIBS=/opt/IntelCPP/lib
LDFLAGS="-L$ICC_LIBS"
SHLIB_CXXLD=icpc

possibly changing ICC_LIBS to wherever you installed it. Benching said rstan package against a clang version with this .R file

stopifnot(require(rstan))
stopifnot(require(parallel))

example(stan_demo)

bench <- function(i) {
  mark <- "elapsed"
  compile <- system.time(fit <- stan_demo(i, chains = 0, iter = 0))[mark]
  execute <- system.time(fit <- stan_demo(i, fit = fit, seed = 12345, refresh = -1))[mark]
  if(length(dim(fit)) == 0) execute <- NA_real_ # failure
  return(c(compile, execute))
}

results <- mclapply(1:length(model_names), mc.cores = 4L, FUN = bench,
                    mc.preschedule = FALSE)

names(results) <- model_names

suggests that Intel might have a slight advantage in computation time.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-tJna6lfy2o4/UJhDHTMNo9I/AAAAAAAAAHA/HlmEhUsduTI/s1600/ClangVsIntel.png>

This is not configuring Eigen to use the Intel Math Library backend and excludes an outlier (schools) that takes more than 1700 seconds for Clang and 2700 seconds for Intel.

If we can get some confirmation on Mac / Windows, we could probably mention the Intel compiler in the manual.

Ben

Con:  breaks backward compatiblity for existing categorical()
       and multinomial()

Over the long haul, I think it's worth changing.  I think
we could fudge updating major version number by calling
it a bug fix, but I'm not too hung up on version numbering one
way or another.

In terms of models, only the BUGS model

   src/models/bugs_examples/vol1/inhalers/inhalers.stan

uses it, and uses the following line to bring it back in
line with the BUGS data:

       response[i, t] - 1 ~ categorical(p[i, t]);

It's also used in eyes.stan as is (without the -1):

   src/models/bugs_examples/vol2/eyes/eyes.stan

The multinomial() isn't used anywhere.  It could've been used
in:

   src/models/bugs_examples/vol2/endo/endo2.stan

but the model was coded directly in terms of its probability
function using lp__ instead of multinomial() -- was this because
mulitnomial()'s behavior was confusing?

- Bob

messages.subject: memory in R and RStan
messages.body_plain:
On 11/12/12 5:37 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> [to stan-dev]
>
> 1. reading csv files of samples in RStan
>
> Currently, no functionality in RStan to do that.  I guess I should work on it so maybe in the release after 1.0.4, we
> can have it.

This would be really useful for scalability in R or even
just for running from Stan command line and then
reading into R for later analysis.

> 2. keeping `samples so far'
>
> I do not know now.  I have never encounter an error in R of `out of memory`.

Lucky you.

If you use 32-bit R and try to run JAGS models,
you'll run into it fast enough.   I rewrote some models in
Stan that took up way less memory than their JAGS counterparts
in R.

Any model that calls iterative solvers on matrices may
take up a lot of memory during sampling the way things are
implemented now.  The issue is that we build up the entire
expression tree over the iterations before propagating the
chain rule backwards for calculating gradients.  We plan to
make this more efficient by extracting the double values,
calling the iterative algorithsm on those, then partially
evaluating the gradients using all the rules in The Matrix
Cookbook and Magnus and Neudecker's book.

> I do not know how R or OS deals with this
> case.  And in the case if it is R calling a C++ function that is running out of memory, I am not sure we can do
> something in R then.

It's going to be handled by process.  When R calls the
C function, it's all in the same process, and so sharing
all the memory from the OSes point of view.  Thus if you run
R in 32-bit mode, the OS is going to put a low ceiling on
how much memory can be used.  A C function called from R
might not be well behaved with respect to R -- it can call its
own malloc() and play havoc with R's memory model.

I don't know how well Rcpp deals with these issues and how
much is up to the user.

You can try something like object.size() in R.  memory.profile()
also looks useful.

There may also be extra objects hanging around in the R environment
taking up space that have nothing to do with Stan.  R uses
garbage collection, but doesn't appear to do it very well.  So
one probably shouldn't use long-running R sessions even if you get
rid of local variables and call gc() to try to clean things up.

 > In short, it is difficult.  Unless this happens a lot, I would not put the investigation on top
> priority.

We should probably test the scalability to make sure we're
not doing something sub-optimally.  If it's a deep issue with
R, I agree that it's not a priority for us to try to fix it!

- Bob

messages.subject: matrix notation
messages.body_plain:
The topic of matrix literals came up on the users list,
and I want to make a concrete proposal that won't be too
difficult to implement.

VECTOR, ROW VECTOR, MATRIX
----------------------------------------

The syntax is pretty simple modulo size conformance
checking.  Here's the BNF:

   matrix_expression ::= '[' matrix_row (';' matrix_row)* ']'

   matrix_row ::= expression*

The idea is that the expressions are laid out in a row
and a ';' indicates to start a new row.

The basic cases are as follows:

   [1 2 3]    : row_vector[3]

   [1 2 3; 4 5 6]  : matrix[2,3]

Use transpose to create vectors:

   [1 2 3]'   : vector[3]

And allow more complex things in a matrix_row in the BNF,
such as a sequence of vectors:

   [[1 2 3]' [4 5 6]']  : matrix[3,2]

In general, we could allow matrices, too:

   [[1 2; 3 4] [5 6; 7 8]] : matrix[4,2]

This would keep nesting in the obvious ways.

ARRAYS
------------------------

We need some way to call out arrays and allow higher
dimensions, so we can't overload the same syntax.
I like the following:

    array ::= 'a' '(' expression* ')'

Examples are:

   a(1,2,3)   :  int[3]

   a(1.0,2,3)  :  real[3]

   a(a(1,2,3), a(4,5,6)) : int[2,3]

   a([1 2 3], [4 5 6]) : row_vector[3][2]

But it brings up type inference issues, because
a(1,2,3) is int[3], not real[3].   We could
add primitive 1D-array syntax such as:

            | 'ints' '(' int_expression* ')'
            | 'reals' '(' real_expression* ')'

Comments?

- Bob

On 11/14/12 11:45 PM, Yuanjun Gao wrote:
> Dear Bob and Daniel,
>
> While I am reading the implementation of nuts_diag, I found something weird for me and I think there might be some flaws
> in the implementation. So I hope you can help me to check.
>
> First, in stan/mcmc/util.hpp, the implementation of "rescaled_leapfrog" seems strange. based on R.Neal's paper
> (2.28)-(2.30), the step_sizes(which is just the inverse mass), should only appear when calculating the new position, but
> shouldn't appear when calculating the new momentum. So I think for the 89th and 99th line, the step_sizes[i] shouldn't
> appear. Right? I paste the code in until.hpp as follows
>
> 86  for (size_t i = 0; i < m.size(); i++)
> 87  m[i] += 0.5 * epsilon * step_sizes[i] * g[i];
> 88  for (size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); i++)
> 89  x[i] += epsilon * step_sizes[i] * m[i];
> 90  double logp;
> 91  try {
> 92  logp = model.grad_log_prob
> <http://mc-stan.org/api/classstan_1_1model_1_1prob__grad.html#ab460008516b71b39c546526f5faf710b>(x, z, g, output_msgs);
> 93  } catch (std::domain_error e <http://mc-stan.org/api/namespacestan_1_1math.html#a3b650a0131d41167ef4837ecc7d02be5>) {
> 94 write_error_msgs <http://mc-stan.org/api/namespacestan_1_1mcmc.html#a50d1d353df9107598d29b6d79f10cd91>(error_msgs,e);
> 95  logp = -std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();
> 96  }
> 97  for (size_t i = 0; i < m.size(); i++)
> 98  m[i] += 0.5 * epsilon * step_sizes[i] * g[i];
> 99  return logp;

It's a varying step size implementation, not a varying
mass one.  See section 5.4.2.4 of Radford's
paper for a discussion.

Also, back of the envelope, we have a lot of trust
in the way it is now because (1) we've tried it on
a lot of models and verified answers against BUGS,
(2) if it were wrong, we'd see lots of Metropolis
rejections because the Hamiltonian would diverge, and
(3) Matt wrote it.

> Secondly, in "nuts_diag.hpp", in the "build_tree" function, the program calculate newH (the new hamilton quantity) as:
>
> 360  double newH = newlogp - 0.5 * stan::math::dot_self
> <http://mc-stan.org/api/namespacestan_1_1math.html#ac81ab85d390fcb594884773a85fac657>(minus);
>
> But now since the mass matrix is not an identity but a diagonal matrix, we should consider the mass as well, so in this
> case, we should use:
>
> newH = newlogp - 0.5 * sum( mminus[i]^2 / mass[i] ) ; (sorry for being too lazy to translate it into C++ï¿½)
>
> I am looking forward to your reply. Thank you very much!

Again, we're just using varying step sizes.

My understanding of the plan for estimating the mass matrix
is to have a single step size and a mass matrix.  If we do that,
then you need to change the kinetic energy term in the Hamiltonian
and the updates as you suggest.  For the kinetc, it's now

   kinetic energy = p' * inv(M) * p

I also believe the plan for warmup is as follows:

   draw 1--20  with simple step size adaptation
               use draws 1--20 to estimate M

   draw 21--40 with step size adaptation and mass matrix M
               use draws 21--40 for new estimate of M
               (i.e., discard draws 1--20 for the estimate of M)

   draw 41--80 and use these draws for new estimate of M

   ....

Then after warmup, mass matrix M and step size remain fixed.

What I was suggesting as an implementation strategy was to
reimplement a new sampler based on a mass matrix instead of
varying step sizes, then recast what we're doing now as a diagonal
mass matrix, then finally go to a full-blown mass matrix.

- Bob

> The main difference is whether to derive the mode from fundamental or c-mode. I recall trying c-mode, because

I abandoned trying to derive from c-mode, believing it was better to have no indentation than bad indentation. The indentation rules (ignoring comments) seem pretty straightforward. >
>
> Lines ending with ; are complete statements/expr
> Default indentation width = 2
>
> If complete statement, indent at same level as previous complete statement
>
> If not complete statement, then indent to
> open ( or [
>
> <-, ~
> last line + indent
> If previous line ends in {, indent >>
>
> If previous line ends in }, indent <<
> If previous line begins with "for", indent >>

I wasn't thinking that far ahead, but sounds reasonable, as long as it's not too much of a pain. If it is a pain, I'm more than happy not having it in ess. As of right now, both our modes are really lightweight and don't depend on much.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] matrix notation
messages.body_plain:
Python (when building an array with numpy) uses a convention that says
every set of nested brackets creates another dimension.  For instance:

[1,2] - creates a column vector

[[1,2]] - creates a row vector

[ [1,2], [3,4], [5,6] ] - creates a 3x2 matrix

[ [ [1,2], [3,4], [5,6] ], [ [1,2], [3,4], [5,6] ] ] - creates a 2x3x2 ndarray

numpy does it this way because it has to construct its arrays from
constructions of iterable objects in python and can't overload
something like the ';'  to make it clearly.

Personally, I find the ; notation more intuitive for matrices and
vectors, but it doesn't expand consistently to multidimensional
arrays.  We could allow both syntaxes where the ';' syntax would only
really work for 1 and 2D objects.

Regarding arrays vs matrices, I like the 'a' prefix but I would use
the same kind of brackets for both cases to make it easier to switch
between them if people need to.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Wed, Nov 14, 2012 at 1:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> The topic of matrix literals came up on the users list,
> and I want to make a concrete proposal that won't be too
> difficult to implement.
>
>
> VECTOR, ROW VECTOR, MATRIX
> ----------------------------------------
>
> The syntax is pretty simple modulo size conformance
> checking.  Here's the BNF:
>
>   matrix_expression ::= '[' matrix_row (';' matrix_row)* ']'
>
>   matrix_row ::= expression*
>
> The idea is that the expressions are laid out in a row
> and a ';' indicates to start a new row.
>
> The basic cases are as follows:
>
>   [1 2 3]    : row_vector[3]
>
>   [1 2 3; 4 5 6]  : matrix[2,3]
>
> Use transpose to create vectors:
>
>   [1 2 3]'   : vector[3]
>
> And allow more complex things in a matrix_row in the BNF,
> such as a sequence of vectors:
>
>   [[1 2 3]' [4 5 6]']  : matrix[3,2]
>
> In general, we could allow matrices, too:
>
>   [[1 2; 3 4] [5 6; 7 8]] : matrix[4,2]
>
> This would keep nesting in the obvious ways.
>
>
> ARRAYS
> ------------------------
>
> We need some way to call out arrays and allow higher
> dimensions, so we can't overload the same syntax.
> I like the following:
>
>    array ::= 'a' '(' expression* ')'
>
>
> Examples are:
>
>   a(1,2,3)   :  int[3]
>
>   a(1.0,2,3)  :  real[3]
>
>   a(a(1,2,3), a(4,5,6)) : int[2,3]
>
>   a([1 2 3], [4 5 6]) : row_vector[3][2]
>
> But it brings up type inference issues, because
> a(1,2,3) is int[3], not real[3].   We could
> add primitive 1D-array syntax such as:
>
>            | 'ints' '(' int_expression* ')'
>            | 'reals' '(' real_expression* ')'
>
>
> Comments?
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>

> --
>
>

On Thursday, November 15, 2012 3:32:01 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I extracted some top-level to-do items for Stan in no particular

In terms of local priority,

> * covariance matrix w. caching (inverse, determinant, Cholesky)

> * new types: lower triangular (+/- strict), diagonal matrix,
>    symmetric matrix, Cholesky factor of pos-def matrix

I would say that the Cholesky factor type should go in ASAP and before the covariance matrix class stuff. But I'm not sure the other types would add that much value once we have the planned covariance matrix classes. There will be a DiagonalCovarianceMatrix class, and we already have diag_matrix(vector). Rarely is there a need for a symmetric matrix that is not also a covariance matrix or a need for a triangular matrix with negative diagonal elements (and thus is not a Cholesky factor). But maybe the value added would be worth the effort if Eigen supported them directly. Conversely, if we add a Cholesky factor type, then we should also add wishart_cholesky() and inv_wishart_cholesky() densities.

Ben

a natural collector and like to have complete sets :-)

diag_matrix(vector) is very inefficient the way we
do it -- we're still bypassing the expression templates
in Eigen that make it efficient.  We could add an
efficient

    matrix diag_matrix_multiply(vector v, matrix m);

that computes diag_matrix(v) * m directly without blowing
it out. First level would be to use Eigen, second level
would be to write specialized auto-diffs.

I have almost no feeling at all which of these ops will
be useful.  They're very easy to write, though.

 > But maybe the value added would be worth the effort if Eigen supported them directly. Conversely, if
> we add a Cholesky factor type, then we should also add wishart_cholesky() and inv_wishart_cholesky() densities.

Agreed.

- Bob

No, the make install target would be for Stan, but it doesn't have anything inherently to do with R. These days, many libraries (with the notable exception of boost) come with .pc files. For example, the top-level of eigen has a fragment of one:

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp/include-what-you-use$ cat /opt/eigen/eigen3.pc.in
Name: Eigen3
Description: A C++ template library for linear algebra: vectors, matrices, and related algorithms
Requires:
Version: ${EIGEN_VERSION_NUMBER}
Libs:
Cflags: -I${INCLUDE_INSTALL_DIR}

When someone "installs" eigen, this .pc.in <http://pc.in> file gets processed so that ${EIGEN_VERSION_NUMBER} becomes 3.1.x and ${INCLUDE_INSTALL_DIR} becomes whatever is appropriate for that platform (/usr/include/eigen3/ for me) and the .pc file gets put into some canonical location where pkg-config can find it (separate from the rest of the library). Thus, this mechanism is useful for any external program that wants to use a library.

What I am thinking for the case of Stan is that make install would

-- call make bin/stanc{.exe} which also makes libstan
-- autogenerate / process the corresponding libstan.pc file(s)
-- put the libstan.pc file into the place in the filesystem where pkg-config looks for that platform

It isn't even absolutely necessary to move any components of Stan into a different place in the filesystem, although I guess we could have an option for that. We can then bundle the pkg-config-lite program (GPL2+) with RStan. The libstan.pc file would have all the information about directories and flags needed to use Stan, so that something like

g++ -o user_model.o user_model.cpp $(pkg-config --libs --cflags libstan)

would compile. At that point, the RStan package would only need to be a few MB and small enough to go on CRAN, since it wouldn't need copies of Stan / boost / eigen. But, to install RStan the computer would need the same version of Stan installed.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: nondiag leapfrog in HMC
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, November 17, 2012 4:23:43 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Is the Cholesky factorization more stable than
> inversion?

Somewhat. Essentially all inversion subroutines for positive definite matrices do a Cholesky factorization, an inversion of the Cholesky factor, and a product of the inverse Cholesky factor with its transpose. So, inversion somewhat exacerbates whatever imprecision there is, but the main thing is that inversion has two extra steps.

Eigen has a LDL' decomposition that is faster and more precise that the LL' decomposition (because the latter requires sqrts). However, the LDL' decomposition does pivoting (which helps avoid precision loss) so the decomposition is actually PLDL'P' where P is a permutation matrix. So, if we were to go that route, we need to incorporate the P matrix (not that difficult and Eigen optimizes that product).

> Is it straightforward to estimate a
> precision matrix instead of a covariance matrix?

Not from "data".

> Radford's paper doesn't push the equations for
> a mass matrix through the leapfrog, and I don't
> trust myself even to verify you've done the algebra
> right.  It looks OK to me, but could someone else check
> it?  The alternative is to implement the standard
> way and your way and make sure they give you the same
> answers.

It looks okay to me. I actually put something analogous into the reparameterization subsection of the Stan manual a few days ago.

> Good question. I wouldn't mind keeping it with Stan (the Stan google repository). That, of course, means that we'd be committing to it for a while. With merging, yes, I agree. It looks like we were doing very similar things. Are you ok with the licensing we chose for Stan? We could distribute Stan mode under a different license if that makes more sense.

I'm fine with including it as part of official Stan; that seems to make the most sense.  I think the license for the emacs mode should be GPL. It's not that I have a strong preference for that, but it appears that almost every emacs library that I've seen is licensed under the GPL.

Now my version of the mode is derived from c++-mode, and I've merged in all functionality that was in your mode and missing from mine. messages.subject: 3rd-order auto-dif and RM-HMC
messages.body_plain:
As far as calculating general RM-HMC goes,
I worked out how to do third-order auto-dif.  There
are various papers covering it, but I find their
notations all very confusing.

All we need to do is nest reverse-mode inside of two forward
modes.  That is, evaluate forward mode for each pair of
variables x and y, while setting the second-order derivaties
to auto-dif variables so we can calculate their gradients.

Forward-mode auto-dif is much easier to write and much faster
to execute than reverse mode because everything's done on the
stack without building up an expression graph on the heap.

So if we have a node g calculated from two variables, x and y (and
perhaps other things), and want to compute
the second-order partial dx.dy, the data structure
would look like this:

    g = fvar(fvar(value,
                  dnode.dy),
             fvar(dnode.dx,
                  dnode.dx.dy))

Each fvar holds a value and an adjoint, which is the derivative
of the value w.r.t. a given input value.  The top-level nodes
hold derivaties w.r.t. x, whose values are fvars taking
derivatives w.r.t. y.    I find it easiest to think about how
this plays out for the addition and multiplication operators:

   fvar(v1,a1) + fvar(v2,a2) = fvar(v1+v2, a1 + a2);

   fvar(v1,a1) * fvar(v2,a2) = fvar(v1*v2, v1*a2 + a1*v2)

Suppose we have

   g(x,y) = x * y

and we want to take d^2g/dx.dy.  Then we initialize x and
y as follows, based on the schematic given above:

   x ==> fvar(fvar(x,0),fvar(1,0))

   y ==> fvar(fvar(y,1),fvar(0,0))

The product then evaluates to:

   x * y = fvar(fvar(x,0) * fvar(y,1),
                fvar(x,0) * fvar(0,0)  +  fvar(1,0) * fvar(y,1))

         = fvar(fvar(x*y, x*1 + 0*y),
                fvar(x*0, x*0 + 0*0) + fvar(1*y, 1*1 + 0*y))

         = fvar(fvar(x*y,x),
                fvar(0,0) + fvar(y,1))

         = fvar(fvar(x*y,x),
                 fvar(y,1))

Just what we want:

    g = x * y
    dx = y
    dy = x
    dx.dy = 1

To get the third-order derivaties we need to set up
the input variables as auto-dif variables and then
calculate the gradient from the final dx.dy term.

This will wind up doing lots of redundant calculations in
a way described in the paper Matt forwarded to the list
recently (as an aside, I thought their evals were misleading
because they used a naive recursion that could've benefitted
from some simple memoization on the CppAD side).

- Bob

messages.subject: Issues with templated matrix functions
messages.body_plain:
We're having some trouble with the templated matrix functions on Windows using g++ 4.6.3 distributed with Rtools 215. The issues only started happening when I added the -std=c++0x flags to the tests.

A couple of the functions we are having trouble with are elt_multiply() and subtract(). The functions are defined in src/stan/math/matrix.hpp and src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp.

These issues may have also caused bus errors when compiling with the macports g++ 4.6.3 compiler with optimization level 0 on Mac OS X.

I think the compiler under Windows is actually doing the right thing in this case and the other compilers (clang++ on Mac, macports g++ 4.6.3 on Mac) are not as strict. There are templated functions in the stan::agrad namespace that conflicts with the function definitions in stan::math namespace.

For elt_multiply(), the math/matrix.hpp version's signature looks like:
   vector_d elt_multiply(const vector_d& v1, const vector_d& v2);

and the agrad/matrix.hpp version's signature looks like:
    template <typename T1, typename T2>
    inline Eigen::Matrix<stan::agrad::var,Eigen::Dynamic,1>
    elt_multiply(const Eigen::Matrix<T1,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& v1,
                 const Eigen::Matrix<T2,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& v2)

When T1 and T2 are double, the function is defined twice for double vector inputs. I believe this is the cause of the problem in Windows, and it may be the cause of the mysterious bus errors in Mac (but the bus error could be something else).

With all that said, I think the solution to these problems is to:
1) rewrite most of the matrix functionality using templates
2) add tests that instantiates all the different permutations of the inputs and outputs to the functions.

Any takers? Can anyone on another OS verify that the agrad/matrix test fails?

I think Ben and Marcus are the closest to this code, but if there aren't any volunteers, this is critical enough for me to pick it up to starting tomorrow.

Daniel

There are subtle issues with templated functions, their specifications, and overloaded functions with the same function signature. With the c++0x flag turned on, it seems like the templated function is instantiated differently than without the flag. I've been reading through the C++ spec and I don't think the spec is clear on whether the compiler is supposed to find the regular overloaded function first or if it should try to instantiate the template function instead.

> > With all that said, I think the solution to these problems is to:
> > 1) rewrite most of the matrix functionality using templates
> > 2) add tests that instantiates all the different permutations of the inputs and outputs to the functions.
> >
> > Any takers? Can anyone on another OS verify that the agrad/matrix test fails?
>
> make test-unit with CC=g++-4.6 works for me. I can't run the tests under cross-compilation right now, but that appears to be an unrelated problem.
>
> Can't we just eliminate the versions that are defined for doubles?

Almost. The return type should change to be a promoted version of the input arguments so that when 2 double arguments are passed in, the resulting type should be double. In the case of elt_multiply(), we really don't need to have different template functions for a matrix, vector, and row_vector. We should be able to define one templated function to take care of all our cases.

> > I think Ben and Marcus are the closest to this code, but if there aren't any volunteers, this is critical enough for me to pick it up to starting tomorrow.
>
> I can do it, but not having Windows would make it a bit harder to trigger failures such as this.

Ok. If you're not triggering it through Linux, I can start tackling it on the Windows box. By the way, I'm just remoting into a different machine to do it.

messages.body_plain:
I pushed a fix for elt_multiply.  Now I'll go and
do elt_divide and look to see if there are other similar
functions that could cause problems.

Here's the new function, which passes unit tests
math/matrix and agrad/matrix:

    /**
      * Return the elementwise multiplication of the specified
      * matrices.
      *
      * @tparam T1 Type of scalars in first matrix.
      * @tparam T2 Type of scalars in second matrix.
      * @tparam R Row type of both matrices.
      * @tparam C Column type of both matrices.
      * @param m1 First matrix
      * @param m2 Second matrix
      * @return Elementwise product of matrices.
      */
     template <typename T1, typename T2, int R, int C>
     Eigen::Matrix<typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T1,T2>::type, R, C>
     elt_multiply(const Eigen::Matrix<T1,R,C>& m1,
                  const Eigen::Matrix<T2,R,C>& m2) {
       stan::math::validate_matching_dims(m1,m2,"elt_multiply");
       Eigen::Matrix<typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T1,T2>::type, R, C>
         result(m1.rows(),m2.cols());
       for (int i = 0; i < m1.size(); ++i)
         result(i) = m1(i) * m2(i);
       return result;
     }

Eigen was ahead of me and had a constructor that took both rows and
columns even if the matrices are vectors or row vectors.  And our
matching_dims() was already set up to handle the overload.

I love that our code base is getting smaller rather than bigger.
There's some kind of computational "folk theorem" in Andrew's
terminology about big programs.

- Bob

> I just tried test-unit with Clang's version of the C++ standard library. To do this, you need to install it and add

> CFLAGS += -stdlib=libc++
>
> somewhere like make/os_*. But we get errors

Upon further review, these are due to using the .real() method in eigendecompositions. To me, things like

Eigen::EigenSolver<matrix_v> solver(m);
return solver.eigenvectors().real();

are problematic. Either m is symmetric, in which case the calling function should have used the _sym variants, which in turn utilize SelfAdjointEigenSolver, or m is not symmetric in which case just returning the real part is generally not the right answer. I think there are cases where all the eigenvalues happen to be real even though the matrix is asymmetric, but they are not likely to occur when m is a matrix_v and it is not like we are verifying that anyway.

Side note: Another argument against hard-coding vars as doubles is that we can't support densities that involve complex numbers. Not that there are millions of users clamoring for complex number support, but there will probably be one eventually.

Then, there are some parts like this

Eigen::SelfAdjointEigenSolver<matrix_v> solver(m,Eigen::EigenvaluesOnly);
return solver.eigenvalues().real();

where the .real() is just unnecessary because the .eigenvalues() of a SelfAdjointEigenSolver are real by construction.

If I fix all that, then test-unit only has a few (unique) errors, all of which seem to be due to io or gm (full log attached).

This is different behavior rather than dropping
a check.  It's what Eigen does.

Eigen doesn't check that the matrix coming in is
symmetric.  In fact, it guarantees it won't look
above the diagonal, so all that can be empty (or
used for something else as their doc says).

So there are two different methods, really:

    eigenvalues_sym(matrix,...);

    eigenvalues_low_tri_self_adjoint(matrix,...);

First would test for symmetry in the matrix but only use
the lower triangular part.  Second would only use the lower
triangular part.

messages.subject: eigendecomposition symmetric; instantiation model
messages.body_plain:
I'll fix the eigenvalues to have two versions requiring
symmetry, symmetric inputs and self-adjoint inputs.
Both will use Eigen's self-adjoint solver, which mirrors
the lower triangular part of the matrix, but the symmetric
input one will test for symmetry to within a tolerance
(any suggestions?  1E-8 seems reasonable to me.)

I'm afraid the re-templatization of the matrix libs is
going to blow out some compilers.  If so, we'll have to
go to an explicit instantiation model.

The basic code organization that makes most sense to me
is what Vandevoorde and Josuttis outline:

    matrix.hpp       // just the headers
    matrix_def.hpp   // complete header definitions
    matrix_inst.cpp  // explicit instantiations

To build header-only, include matrix_def.hpp.
To build with instantiation, include matrix.hpp and
link against compilation of matrix_inst.cpp.

The major-pain-in-the-ass downside is that you have
to list all of the template instantiations in matrix_inst.cpp.
This is easy for matrix for now with only double and
var.  But when we mix in forward-mode auto-dif, the
combinatorics will be problematic.

- Bob

Daniel's been working on vectorizations, but

We have discussed what needs to be done in general, which is
creating MatrixView and TensorView expression templates along the
same lines as VectorView (and DoubleVectorView):

   VectorView :  T or T[] as T[]

   MatrixView :  T[] or T[,] as T[,]

   TensorView :  T[,] or T[,,] as T[,,]

How much array processing should be built in?   I ask because
there are three ways to shape a vector:

   vector<T>
   Eigen::Matrix<T,Dynamic,1>
   Eigen::Matrix<T,1,Dynamic>

four ways to shape a matrix:

   vector<vector<T> >
   vector<Eigen::Matrix<T,Dynamic,1> >
   vector<Eigen::Matrix<T,1,Dynamic> >
   Eigen::Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic>

and four ways to shape a tensor:

   vector<vector<vector<T> > >
   vector<vector<Eigen::Matrix<T,Dynamic,1> > >
   vector<vector<Eigen::Matrix<T,1,Dynamic> > >
   vector<Eigen::Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic> >

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Rcpp 0.10.1 breaks RcppEigen (Fwd: [Rcpp-devel] Rcpp 0.10.1 and RcppEigen)
messages.body_plain:
As I've been saying for a while now, I
would VERY much like to get rid of the
dependency on RcppEigen and just include our
own copy of the Eigen libs in RStan.

My original reasoning was abstract -- the more
moving parts we can eliminate, the more stable our
software will be.  I was thinking something like this
was inevitable, though I was expecting it to come
from incompatible Eigen versions, not Rcpp breaking
their own dependent module!

Shouldn't be a problem for us to include our own
copy of Eigen if we're not on CRAN.

I think the route to getting to CRAN will be the
one Ben laid out, where we do what JAGS and BUGS
and require an external install of Stan.  I'd
still recommend users to use your all-in-one
installer, but if we want something on CRAN, this
looks like the best route.

Also, though I know it sounds radical at this point,
I'm also thinking it might be simpler in the long
run to NOT have us run inside the R process, but to
just call an external install of Stan (like R2WinBUGs
did).  My original motivation for wanting to do it all
in C++ in a single process was so that we could have
a C++-based representation of the data and samples
and not have ot use R's storage -- that plan went out
the window when we couldn't serialize the state of
a C++ object easily through Rcpp.

- Bob

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ make O=0 CC=clang++ test-unit
clang++ -I src -I lib/eigen_3.1.2 -I lib/boost_1.52.0 -O0 -Wall -Wno-unused-function -Wno-tautological-compare -DGTEST_USE_OWN_TR1_TUPLE -stdlib=libc++   -c -Wno-c++11-extensions -std=c++0x -I lib/gtest_1.6.0/include -I lib/gtest_1.6.0 src/test/io/csv_writer_test.cpp -o test/io/csv_writer.o

messages.body_plain:
Hi stan-dev,

I added a --point_estimate flag that runs Newton's method to find a
maximum of the joint log-likelihood, using finite-differences to
compute the Hessian and an eigendecomposition to adjust it to be
negative definite if necessary.

Is it all right if I push it? I know we don't really want to encourage
people to blindly fit point estimates, but sometimes it's useful to be
able to. For example, I'm currently interested in fitting a model by
maximum marginal likelihood where I can integrate out the hidden
variables.

Maybe we could leave it as an undocumented feature.

Matt

messages.subject: broadcasting for binary ops
messages.body_plain:
On a completely different topic, I have a question
about how general and how implicit to make binary
operations.

R seems very general here (though I wouldn't even
know where to look it up).

As a prelude, I added binary comparison operators
(<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=) and binary logical operators (&&
and ||) and the unary logical operator (!).  They
are defined now in both the parser and in the
C++ implementation to take a pair of double arguments
or a pair of int args (the consequence of this is that
an int and double comparison will promote the int to
a double).

I probably won't get it done and tested for the next
release, but I'd like to be able to use them in the
R style, with code like

    real y[K];
    int z[K];

    z = y > 2 && y < 5;

This requires a version of > that takes an int (or
double) and array as input, and a version of &&
that takes a pair of arrays.  This notion is very general.
We could promote row vectors to matrices by replicating
rows or promote column vectors to matrices to by replicating
the column across the matrix.  We could also have

   vector<vector<double>> == vector<double>

return a vector<vector<int>> by replicating the
vector<double>.

One issue is that we don't have int vectors or matrices,
so if we want to do something like !m, where m is a matrix,
the best we can do is return a 2D array of int.

To do this, we need to do what the Eigen doc calls
"broadcasting" (I can never recall what R calls it):

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TutorialReductionsVisitorsBroadcasting.html#TutorialReductionsVisitorsBroadcastingBroadcasting

I figured out how to do this all with metaprogramming
given just the base operation (I don't know how general
I'll make it, but I'm starting with binary ops).

What I want to know is how general people think the
definitions should be.

We could require the vector to matrix broadcasts,
which seem the most confusing, to be explicit.  Or
I could just restrict it to the case where either the
arguments were the same dimensionality or one was
a simple scalar or int.

Once I build the metaprograms, it should be simple to
extend this kind of thing to all of our binary and
unary functions.  (Ternary might be tricky.)  I'm still
absolutely giddy with delight at how nice our current
probability functions look and how efficient they are.
We don't need as much work for the binary ops, because
they return multivariates, which won't allow us to save
on auto-dif (at least not easily) the way we do in the
probability functions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] broadcasting for binary ops
messages.body_plain:
The numpy library for python does a very general form of broadcasting like this.  For a general ND array, al singleton dimensions can get broadcast up to the size of the corresponding dimensions in the other array.  It's a really nice feature, but it is primarily for efficiencies which we are unlikely to realize.

I would say focus on broadcasting for the scalar vs vector/matrix/array case.  This is consistent with what we're already doing for scalar-matrix/vector ops +, -, * and /.

Cheers,
Marcus

> release, but I'd like to be able to use them in the
> R style, with code like
>
>    real y[K];
>    int z[K];
>
>    z = y > 2 && y < 5;
>
> This requires a version of > that takes an int (or
> double) and array as input, and a version of &&
> that takes a pair of arrays.  This notion is very general.
> We could promote row vectors to matrices by replicating
> rows or promote column vectors to matrices to by replicating
> the column across the matrix.  We could also have
>
>   vector<vector<double>> == vector<double>
>
> return a vector<vector<int>> by replicating the
> vector<double>.
>
> One issue is that we don't have int vectors or matrices,
> so if we want to do something like !m, where m is a matrix,
> the best we can do is return a 2D array of int.
>
> To do this, we need to do what the Eigen doc calls
> "broadcasting" (I can never recall what R calls it):
>
> http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TutorialReductionsVisitorsBroadcasting.html#TutorialReductionsVisitorsBroadcastingBroadcasting
>
> I figured out how to do this all with metaprogramming
> given just the base operation (I don't know how general
> I'll make it, but I'm starting with binary ops).
>
> What I want to know is how general people think the
> definitions should be.
>
> We could require the vector to matrix broadcasts,
> which seem the most confusing, to be explicit.  Or
> I could just restrict it to the case where either the
> arguments were the same dimensionality or one was
> a simple scalar or int.
>
> Once I build the metaprograms, it should be simple to
> extend this kind of thing to all of our binary and
> unary functions.  (Ternary might be tricky.)  I'm still
> absolutely giddy with delight at how nice our current
> probability functions look and how efficient they are.
> We don't need as much work for the binary ops, because
> they return multivariates, which won't allow us to save
> on auto-dif (at least not easily) the way we do in the
> probability functions.

>
>
> - Bob
>
> --
>
>

messages.subject: Re: optimization
messages.body_plain:
Not sure of the background of this discussion on optimization, but I see below talk of MLE and functions without analytic derivatives.

I do MLE optimisation in high dimensions, and currently use a heuristic algorithm (mainly DE) followed by BOBYQA. Neither needs derivatives. Once I have worked out the analytical derivative, I will use L-BFGS-B (I have converted from Fortran to Java) and maybe even a NUTS sampler, but still probably keep the initial heuristic algorithm.

My point is, if you are looking to do Newton type methods without derivatives, BOBYQA from one of optimizations gradfathers, Powell, is worth looking at. Originally Fortran, but there is a Java version from Apache.

messages.subject: Re: optimization
messages.body_plain:
The nice thing about working in Stan is that you don't have to write
down (or even be able to write down) the derivatives—it uses automatic
differentiation to compute the derivatives of the log-joint function.
So if your model includes functions that are continuously
differentiable but whose derivatives don't have a closed form then
Stan can still compute those derivatives. It looks like BOBYQA is more
for the scenario where you only have an oracle that evaluates the
objective function; in Stan we have direct access to the objective
function, so we can take a more direct route.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: optimization
messages.body_plain:
The auto-diff does analytic derivatives on the program.
There's a pretty good description on the Wikipedia:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation

We use reverse mode with a templated C++ implementation of
what they call taping.

Basically, anything where you can code the probability
function in C++, we can differentiate it (as can the other
auto-diff packages).  You can use loops, recursion, function
calls, whatever.  You do have to either (a) use one of
the functions in our library, or (b) use something that
templates the variables for which you want to take the gradient.

The penalty in speed is about a factor of four over just
the probability function. This is independent of
dimension (unlike finite diffs, which is slow in every implementation and
even slower if you do something less naive than a single
point).  Space usage can be bad for iterative
algorithms because it stores the entire expression tree leading
to the log probability in a forward pass before applying the
chain rule in a backward pass.

- Bob
